passage:
“Aadhya moved to another table today,” said Yash, pushing his rice around his plate.
“Did you two argue?” asked Mummy.
“About who gets to be science partner.”
“What do you think her moving means?”
“Maybe she's angry. Or hurt.” Yash frowned. “Or maybe she just wants space.”
“Could be any of those. What might help?”
“Not chasing her, I guess. I could leave a note.”
“Good idea.”
He tore a page from his notebook. “Sorry about the science thing. Sit with me if you like.” He smiled a little.

qa.q: What did Yash and Aadhya argue about?
qa.a: They argued about who gets to be science partner.

qa.q: What does Yash think Aadhya's move to another table might mean?
qa.a: That she might be angry or hurt, or might just want space. He does not decide which, since a move could mean any of those.

qa.q: What could help repair the friendship?
qa.a: A kind note and an open invitation, as Yash writes, and not chasing or pushing her, so Aadhya can come back in her own time.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel when she finds the note?
qa.a: Perhaps relieved and a bit touched that Yash respected her space. She may still need time before she sits with him.

grounding: A friend moves to another table after an argument; a kind note repairs more than pushing.

passage: After Rehana and I argued about the rules of the game, she picked up her lunch box and moved to the next table. I felt my stomach drop. I thought she hated me. I wanted to run over, but Mum had told me that sometimes a friend just needs space. So I wrote a note and slipped it into her bag: “I'm sorry I shouted. You can sit with me whenever you want. Jyoti.” The next day she came and sat down. She said, “I was hurt, but I also needed some time to cool down.” I was glad I hadn't chased her.

qa.q: Where did Rehana move after the argument?
qa.a: She moved to the next table with her lunch box.

qa.q: What did Jyoti think Rehana's move meant, and what did Rehana say later?
qa.a: At first Jyoti thought Rehana hated them. Rehana said she was hurt and also needed time to cool down, so it was both hurt and a need for space.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Jyoti left a kind note with an open invitation instead of chasing, which gave Rehana space and a way back.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt finding the note in her bag?
qa.a: Probably touched and relieved that Jyoti said sorry without pushing. It made it easier to come back the next day.

grounding: A friend moves away after an argument, which may mean hurt or a need for space; a kind note helps.

passage: Lunch note, Friday. Ayesha, class teacher. On Wednesday, Aadhya and Tanya argued over the art project. On Thursday at lunch, Tanya picked up her tiffin and moved to the far table. Aadhya noticed at once. She followed Tanya three times, sitting down beside her and saying, “Just talk to me!” Each time Tanya turned her back or moved again. I called Aadhya over. I said Tanya might be angry, or hurt, or just need space, and following her might feel like pushing. Aadhya's eyes filled, but she sat with me. At the end of the day she wrote a note: Sorry about the project. Sit together tomorrow? This morning they came in together.

qa.q: How many times did Aadhya follow Tanya at lunch?
qa.a: Aadhya followed Tanya three times.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she kept following Tanya?
qa.a: Aadhya felt hurt and anxious to fix things, and her eyes filled when asked to stop.

qa.q: Why did the note work better than following?
qa.a: It gave Tanya space and a kind invitation she could accept in her own time, instead of pushing her to talk.

qa.q: What might Tanya's move to the far table have meant?
qa.a: Tanya may have been angry or hurt, or simply needed space after the argument.

grounding: Shows a child noticing a friend moving away after an argument, and a kind note later repairing more than pushing.

passage: Tuesday. Manoj's diary. At the bus stop, Nikita stood at the far end, back turned, earphones in. Yesterday in class I laughed when she said Mount Everest was in Africa, and everyone else laughed too. Her face went red, and she hasn't sat next to me since. I wanted to go over and say sorry right away, but I thought if I pushed, she'd just walk off. So I didn't. After school I wrote on a chit: Sorry I laughed. I get stuff wrong all the time. Cricket on Saturday? I gave it to her sister to pass on. Tonight her sister told me Nikita smiled.

qa.q: What had Nikita said about Mount Everest?
qa.a: Nikita said Mount Everest was in Africa.

qa.q: What might Nikita be feeling as she stood with her back turned?
qa.a: She is probably hurt and embarrassed about being laughed at, and may want space rather than an instant apology.

qa.q: Why was Manoj's chit a good choice?
qa.a: It apologised kindly and offered an invitation without pushing, letting Nikita respond when ready.

qa.q: What would change if Manoj had rushed over at the bus stop?
qa.a: Nikita might have felt cornered and walked off, and the hurt could have lasted longer.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend turning away after a conflict as hurt, and choosing a kind note and invitation over pushing.

passage: After the argument about whose turn it was to row, Siddharth moved to the far end of his uncle's fishing boat and sat with his back to Maria, staring at the water. Maria's first thought was, Fine, be like that. Her second was worse: Maybe he'll never talk to me again. She almost crawled over the nets to argue some more. Instead she remembered what her grandmother said: “Some people need the sea between them for a while.” She left him alone until the boat reached the shore. Then she held out half of her raw mango with salt and chilli. “Row tomorrow? You first.” Siddharth took it. “You first,” he said.

qa.q: What did Maria hold out to Siddharth?
qa.a: She held out half of her raw mango with salt and chilli.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when Siddharth turned his back?
qa.a: Maria felt annoyed at first, then worried he might never talk to her again.

qa.q: Why did waiting and then offering the mango work?
qa.a: It gave Siddharth space until the shore and then a kind invitation, which repaired more than arguing would have.

qa.q: What might Siddharth have needed at the far end of the boat?
qa.a: Siddharth may have been angry or hurt and needed some space to calm down before talking.

grounding: Shows a child noticing a friend moving away after an argument, giving space and repairing with a later invitation.

passage:
In their Stockholm classroom, Emeka and Oskar had been building the volcano together for a week. Then Emeka called Oskar's lava idea "dumb". Oskar went red, picked up his paints and moved to the table by the window, his back turned.

Emeka stared at that back all afternoon. At pickup he wanted to run after him and say, "Just talk to me!" His older sister shook her head. "Maybe he needs space. Try something small."

That night Emeka wrote on a card: "Sorry I said dumb. Your lava idea was good. Paint it together tomorrow?" He slid it into Oskar's cubby in the morning. By break, Oskar's paints were back on their table.

qa.q: Where did Oskar move to?
qa.a: The table by the window.

qa.q: What was Oskar most likely feeling when he moved away and turned his back?
qa.a: Hurt and angry that his idea was called dumb; he may also simply have needed space to calm down.

qa.q: Why did the card work better than chasing Oskar at pickup?
qa.a: It gave Oskar space, apologised clearly and made a friendly invitation, instead of pushing him to talk before he was ready.

qa.q: How did Emeka's sister see the situation?
qa.a: She saw that Oskar might need space and that pushing could make it worse, so she suggested something small.

grounding: It shows a child noticing a friend move tables and turn away after an argument, and a kind note later repairing more than pushing.
